```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# Load your data here
# 1. Load data
df <- read_csv("data/hd_mortalitybyca.csv")
dz_codes <- read_csv("data/dz_codes.csv")

# 2. Create Council Area lookup table
area <- dz_codes %>%
  select(CA, CAName) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  drop_na(CA, CAName)

# 3. Clean and prepare mortality data
final_df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    year_provisional = str_ends(Year, "p"),
    year = as.integer(str_remove(Year, "p"))
  ) %>%
  rename(
    age_group = AgeGroup,
    gender = Sex,
    diagnosis = Diagnosis,
    deaths = NumberOfDeaths,
    crude_rate = CrudeRate,
    easr = EASR,
    ca = Ca
  ) %>%
  left_join(area, by = c("ca" = "CA")) %>%
  mutate(
    area = if_else(
      ca == "S92000003",
      "Scotland",
      CAName
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    year, year_provisional,
    ca, area,
    age_group, gender, diagnosis,
    deaths, crude_rate, easr
  )

# 4. Validate cleaned data
stopifnot(nrow(final_df) == nrow(df))
stopifnot(!anyNA(final_df$area))
stopifnot(!anyNA(final_df$year))


# 5.filter CHD
chd_df <- final_df %>%
  filter(diagnosis == "Coronary Heart Disease")
```

## Research Question


### **How did coronary heart disease mortality in Scotland change between 2015 and 2023, and how do age, sex and council area shape these trends?**

**Why it matters:**

- Identifying most vulnerable groups.

- Highlighting regions with disproportionately higher mortality rates.

- Helping policymakers and healthcare provider better allocate resources.

- Designing targeted interventions to reduce heart disease mortality.

---

## Data

**Source:** Public Health Scotland - Heart Disease Mortality by Council Area

- **Coverage:** 32 Council Areas + Scotland aggregate, 2015-2024

- **Variables:** year, area, age group, sex, deaths, crude rate, EASR

- **Note:** **2024 figures are provisional**, so they are excluded from modelling (models use 2015-2023)

- **Cleaning:** joined the Data Zone 2022 lookupdictionary to convert alphanumeric zone codes into readable Council Area names, filtered specifically for CHD

---

class: center, middle

## Exploratory Data Analysis

---

### National Trend of Coronary Heart Disease Mortality (2015-2024)

.pull-left[
```{r national-trend-plot, echo=FALSE}
# National trend chart
time_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    area == "Scotland",
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  ) %>%
  arrange(year)
# The number of deaths from coronary heart disease in Scotland nationwide from 2015 to 2024
ggplot(time_df, aes(x = year, y = easr)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2024) +
  labs(
    subtitle = "European Age-Standardised Rate, 2015–2024 (2024 provisional)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "EASR (per 100,000)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
]

.pull-right[
- **National baseline:** CHD mortality across Scotland declined steadily from 2015 to 2024

- **Recent trend:** A slight flattening around 2020-2021

- *(2024 data are provisional)*
]

### Geographical Differences Across Council Areas

<style>
.pull-left { width: 48% !important; }
.pull-right { width: 48% !important; }
</style>

.pull-left[
```{r geography-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5}
# Area data table
geographical_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    area != "Scotland",
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  ) %>%
  group_by(area) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_easr = mean(easr, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_easr))

geographical_highlight_df <- geographical_df %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_easr)) %>%
  mutate(
    rank = row_number(),
    highlight_group = case_when(
      rank <= 5 ~ "Top 5",
      rank > n() - 5 ~ "Bottom 5",
      TRUE ~ "Middle"
    )
  )
geographical_top_bottom <- geographical_highlight_df %>%
  filter(highlight_group != "Middle")

# Regional Average Charts for Deaths from Coronary Heart Disease from 2015 to 2023
ggplot(
  geographical_top_bottom,
  aes(
    x = reorder(area, mean_easr),
    y = mean_easr,
    fill = highlight_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(mean_easr, 1)),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Top 5" = "#D55E00",
      "Bottom 5" = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  expand_limits(
    y = max(geographical_top_bottom$mean_easr) * 1.12
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Geographical Differences in CHD Mortality",
    subtitle = "Top 5 and Bottom 5 Council Areas, 2015–2023",
    x = "Council Area",
    y = "Mean annual EASR (per 100,000)",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r geography-trend-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5}
# The variation curves of coronary heart disease deaths across different regions over time (using the annual EASR data)
geographical_trend_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    area != "Scotland",
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  ) %>%
  inner_join(
    geographical_top_bottom %>%
      select(area, highlight_group),

  group_by(year, highlight_group) %>%

    mean_easr = mean(easr, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Drawings (without any weighting based on the actual population of the region; it’s simply a simple arithmetic calculation)
ggplot(
  geographical_trend_df,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = mean_easr,
    color = highlight_group
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Top 5" = "#D55E00",
      "Bottom 5" = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "CHD Mortality Trends in High- and Low-Mortality Areas",
    subtitle = "Five highest vs five lowest mean-EASR Council Areas, 2015–2023",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean annual EASR (per 100,000)",
    color = "Area Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```
]

- **Subset analysis:** We compared the 5 highest-mortality authorities vs. the five lowest-mortality authorities. 

- ** Regional Disparity:** High-mortality areas (e.g. East Ayrshire, Glasgow City) experienced nearly **double** the rate of lowest-mortality ares.
- **Persistence:** This regional gap persisted throughout 2015–2023.

## Linear Regression Analysis

```{r regression-data, echo=FALSE}
# Use the 10 selected Council Areas
regression_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    area %in% geographical_top_bottom$area,
    age_group == "All Ages",
    gender == "All"
  )
```

---

### Regional Modelling: Simple vs. Multiple Linear Regression

```{r simple-regression, echo=FALSE}
# Simple linear regression
model1 <- lm(easr ~ year, data = regression_df)
```

.pull-left[
```{r simple-regression-plot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(regression_df, aes(x = year, y = easr)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple Linear Regression",
    subtitle = "CHD mortality rates in 10 Council Areas",
    x = "Year",
    y = "EASR (per 100,000)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```
]

```{r multiple-regression, echo=FALSE}
# Multiple linear regression
model2 <- lm(easr ~ year + area, data = regression_df)
```

.pull-right[
```{r multiple-regression-plot, echo=FALSE}
# Calculate predicted mortality rates
regression_df$predicted_easr <- predict(model2)

# Plot predicted trends for each area
ggplot(regression_df,
       aes(x = year, y = predicted_easr,
           color = area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2023) +
  labs(
    title = "Multiple Linear Regression",
    subtitle = "Predicted CHD mortality trends by Council Area",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Predicted EASR (per 100,000)",
    color = "Council Area"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```
]

- **Model 1(Year only):**  $R^2 = 0.017$, $p = 0.216$.  Year alone cannot adequately explain the variation.

- **Model 2(Year + Area):** Adding Council Area increased $R^2$ to **0.743** and reduced the residual SE to 17.796. 

- **Conclusion:** This confirms that regional disparities account for the majority of variation across these areas.

---

### Actual vs Predicted Mortality Rates

```{r predicted-vs-actual, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(regression_df,
       aes(x = easr, y = predicted_easr)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    subtitle = "Multiple Linear Regression",
    x = "Actual EASR (per 100,000)",
    y = "Predicted EASR (per 100,000)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The dashed red line represents perfect predictions. Points closer to this line indicate smaller prediction errors.

---

### Demographic Modelling: Age, Sex, and Interaction Effects

```{r gender-year model,echo =FALSE}
# Data organization – Age groups
demographic_df <- chd_df %>%
  filter(
    area == "Scotland",
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2023,
    age_group %in% c(
      "0-44 years",
      "45-64 years",
      "65-74 years",
      "75plus years"
    ),
    gender %in% c("Male", "Female")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    age_group = factor(
      age_group,
      levels = c(
        "0-44 years",
        "45-64 years",
        "65-74 years",
        "75plus years"
      )
    ),
# Data organization – Sex groups
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = c("Female", "Male")
    ),
    year_centered = year - 2015
  )

model3 <- lm(
  crude_rate ~ year_centered + age_group + gender,
  data = demographic_df
)


```


```{r model4, echo = FALSE}
#model4 
model4 <- lm(
  crude_rate ~ year_centered + age_group * gender,
  data = demographic_df
)

# Model 4 shows good fitting performance; the Adjusted R-squared value increases to over 99%. However, there are still issues. That is, the assumption that the female mortality rate decreases by 0–44 per year leads to a negative mortality rate in the end.
```


```{r demographic-model-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.5}
# Preparing data
demographic_comparison_df <- demographic_df %>%
  mutate(
    model3_fitted = fitted(model3),
    model4_fitted = fitted(model4)
  ) %>%
  select(
    year, age_group, gender,
    crude_rate, model3_fitted, model4_fitted
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(crude_rate, model3_fitted, model4_fitted),
    names_to = "source",
    values_to = "rate"
  )
# Draw Chart 1
ggplot(
  demographic_comparison_df,
  aes(x = year, y = rate, color = source)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dotted",
    color = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = source), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = demographic_comparison_df %>%
      filter(source == "crude_rate"),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  facet_grid(age_group ~ gender, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "crude_rate" = "grey30",
      "model3_fitted" = "#D55E00",
      "model4_fitted" = "#0072B2"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "crude_rate" = "Observed",
      "model3_fitted" = "Model 3",
      "model4_fitted" = "Model 4"
    )
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "crude_rate" = "solid",
      "model3_fitted" = "dashed",
      "model4_fitted" = "dashed"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2015, 2019, 2023)) +
  labs(
    subtitle = "Observed and fitted CHD mortality rates, 2015–2023",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mortality Rate (per 100,000)",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Note: Y-axis scales differ between age groups."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

- **Model 3(Additive):** Assumes a constant mortality gap. The sex gap widens from **3.45** (0-44 years) to **419.57** (75plus years) per 100,000.
- **Model 4(Interaction):** Adding an age-sex interaction term significantly improves model fit ($F = 136.84$, $p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$).

---

### Model Diagnostics

```{r Test, echo = FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=3.5}
diagnostic_df <- regression_df %>%
  mutate(
    fitted_value = fitted(model2),
    residual = residuals(model2)
  )
ggplot(
  diagnostic_df,
  aes(x = year, y = residual)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~area, ncol = 5) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals over Time by Council Area",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

- **Temporal Autocorrelation in Model 2:** Plotting residuals over time across the 10 Council Areas reveals noticeable temporal patterns and positive lag-1 autocorrelation in several regions, indicating multi-year local fluctuations that a single linear slope cannot fully capture.

- **Heteroscedasticity and Boundary Issues in Model 4:** Variance increasing with higher mortality rates in older age groups; p-values should be interpreted with caution. Fitted values for 0-44 years females eventually fall below zero, which is impossible for a mortality rate.

---

## Summary of Findings

- **Geographical Variation:** Adding Council Area to the regional regression model increased $R^2$ from 0.017 to 0.743 (and adjusted $R^2$ from 0.006 to 0.711), while reducing the residual standard error from 32.986 to 17.796. This confirms that regional disparities account for the majority of variation across these areas.

- **Demographic Interaction:** Incorporating the interaction between age group and sex significantly improved the demographic model ($R^2 = 0.9937$), demonstrating that the excess mortality experienced by males widens substantially in middle and older age groups rather than remaining constant.

---

## Limitations and Ethical Considerations

- **Subset Selection:** The regional regression models only included ten Council Areas selected from the highest and lowest mortality extremes. Therefore, the findings may not represent intermediate regions across Scotland.

- **Linear Model Assumptions:** Assuming a single constant annual slope across all regions and demographic cohorts can lead to residual autocorrelation and unrealistic negative rate predictions in low-mortality groups (0-44 years females). Future work could apply Poisson or generalised linear models to address non-negativity and heteroscedasticity.

- **Aggregated Data and Ethics:** Because the dataset consists of publicly available, aggregated population statistics from Public Health Scotland, there are no individual privacy concerns. However, because the data are aggregated at the Council Area level, we cannot infer individual-level risk factors (such as smoking or socioeconomic deprivation), and care should be taken to interpret regional differences in terms of healthcare resource allocation rather than stigmatising specific communities.
